article_title: Broadening Participation in STEM College Majors: Effects of Attending a STEM-Focused High School
citation: Means, Wang, Wei, Iwatani, & Peters. (2018). Broadening Participation in STEM College Majors: Effects of Attending a STEM-Focused High School. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418806305
title: Common design features of inclusive STEM high schools
description: The article enumerates the features ISHSs tend to share even though curriculum and instructional practices vary: "a rigorous STEm-focused college preparatory curriculum for all students; use of project- or problem-based pedagogy; an extensive network of supports for students who need assistance mastering the curriculum; incorporation of career, technology, and life skills; supportive school climate; and partnerships with external organizations to support out-of-school STEm experiences." Some states, including Texas, have codified these features in school designation guidelines.

constraints: Curriculum and instructional practices may vary across different ISHSs
target_learners: High school students from groups under-represented in STEM fields
target_learning_goals: STEM college readiness and STEM career interest
examples: Texas T-STEM academies follow a blueprint calling for mechanisms enabling students to earn 12 or more college credits during high school

article_title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction
citation: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph.
title: Three-dimension, three-level evaluation rubric for Technological Isomorphism Awareness
description: The article's Table 4 rubric: "The evaluation framework for this lesson focuses on three progressive dimensions, with each dimension structured across three proficiency levels." The dimensions are Data Literacy & Statistical Reasoning (assessed via accuracy of manually plotted graphs and classroom discourse analysis), AI Cognitive Understanding (post-test open-ended questionnaire), and Ethical and Boundary Awareness (verbal behavior during reflection on prediction failures). Level 3 of AI Cognitive Understanding is treated as an observable indicator of activated awareness, and Level 3 of Ethical and Boundary Awareness indicates progression toward boundary-sensitive understanding.
requirements: Educators conduct qualitative assessments through structured classroom observations and brief post-lesson interviews
constraints: Evaluation of student cognitive shifts relied predominantly on qualitative discourse analysis and observational indicators; the authors call for standardized psychometric instruments
target_learners: elementary mathematics students in AI-integrated lessons
target_learning_goals: ethical and boundary awareness of AI
examples: Teachers are told to attend to whether students spontaneously produce contextual attributions such as 'Because it didn't know the lid was opened!' during anomalous data segments

article_title: Embodied Inquiry with AI as Facilitator: An Exploratory Case Study
citation: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://udlguidelines.cast.org
title: ISLE (Investigative Science Learning Environment): inquiry organized around observational, testing and application experiments
description: ISLE is an approach to physics teaching in which students build and test physics knowledge the way physicists do, starting from phenomena they observe with their own eyes and hands. It is organized around three kinds of experiment: observational experiments where students look for patterns and propose multiple explanations; testing experiments where each explanation is put at risk in hypothetico-deductive form, aiming to falsify; and application experiments where the surviving model solves a practical problem. In this study, the laboratory session on statics of fluids followed the ISLE sequence, with the AI facilitator configured to follow it. It rests on four foundations: the epistemology of physics, findings of cognitive science, theories of learning communities, and universal design.
requirements: Students work through the process in small groups and express ideas in multiple representations: words, diagrams, graphs and equations, and in practice gestures as well
constraints: The structure of ISLE derives from how physics itself produces knowledge, not from a general theory of learning; its family resemblance with Kolb's cycle is a resonance rather than a foundation
target_learners: university students in physics education, many of whom intend to become teachers
target_learning_goals: learning physics by building and testing models like physicists
thinking scientifically through observation, testing and application experiments
examples: Students first explored how pressure grows with depth in water, then used a dynamometer to weigh objects at different depths to construct the buoyant force model F = ρ·g·V
key_sources: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21349

article_title: Embodied Inquiry with AI as Facilitator: An Exploratory Case Study
citation: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://udlguidelines.cast.org
title: Bridge between ISLE multiple representations, multimodal resources, and UDL multiple means, read through the interactionist embodiment tradition
description: The authors propose a bridge, offered as an interpretive inference rather than an established equivalence: what physics education research calls multiple representations, and social semiotics calls multimodal resources, is what Universal Design for Learning calls multiple means. Their primary lens is the interactionist tradition of embodiment research, in which meaning is built between people as they talk, gesture and act together, so the meaning of a laboratory activity lives in the interaction rather than inside individual heads or the worksheet. Read this way, the UDL Guidelines 3.0, with their principle of multiple means of action and expression, describe from the side of inclusion what ISLE describes from the side of physics practice: a learning environment that keeps many channels for meaning open.
requirements: A learning environment that keeps many channels for meaning open, rather than privileging the verbal one
constraints: The bridge is an interpretive inference of the authors rather than an established equivalence
target_learners: university students, including those served by inclusive design in higher education
target_learning_goals: becoming fluent in a critical constellation of modes of disciplinary discourse: words, diagrams, graphs, mathematics, apparatus and actions
examples: ISLE group work in the study, where students point, manipulate, sketch and gesture as ways of thinking together

article_title: ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents
citation: YoungHoon Jeon, Suwan Kim, Haein Son, Sookbun Lee, Yeil Jeong, Unggi Lee. (2026). ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10620
title: ISD-Agent-Bench: 25,795-scenario benchmark with multi-judge evaluation for LLM-based ISD agents
description: ISD-Agent-Bench is a large-scale benchmark of instructional-design scenarios built by combining a Context Axis of educational settings with an ISD Axis of 33 ADDIE-based sub-steps. The article states it is "the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-based ISD agents", constructed "with 25,795 scenarios and 1,202 test cases, featuring stratified sampling across 9 contextual dimensions". Evaluation combines ADDIE rubric assessment (70%) with trajectory evaluation (30%) using a cross-provider multi-judge protocol achieving 0.905 inter-judge reliability.
requirements: Scenarios require LLM-based generation from seed abstracts plus rule-based and LLM-based validation stages to ensure logical consistency
constraints: Seed abstracts show domain concentration, with education-specific (1.9%) and healthcare (0.1%) domains underrepresented
target_learners: Learners across all context-axis categories: teens to adults over 40, K-12 through corporate and vocational settings
target_learning_goals: Instructional systems design across the full ADDIE lifecycle: analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation
examples: The dataset includes a representative Hard scenario: designing a game-based business leadership course for corporate professionals in an online synchronous environment with gamification required and 2-4 weeks duration

article_title: ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents
citation: YoungHoon Jeon, Suwan Kim, Haein Son, Sookbun Lee, Yeil Jeong, Unggi Lee. (2026). ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10620
title: Four ISD theory-based agents (React-ADDIE, ADDIE-Agent, Dick-Carey-Agent, RPISD-Agent) grounded in classical ISD theories
description: The article develops four LLM agents grounded in classical ISD theories: React-ADDIE "integrates the classical ADDIE framework with ReAct-style reasoning" using 5 phase-level tools; ADDIE-Agent implements the five-phase sequential workflow with 14 specialized tools; Dick-Carey-Agent follows the nine-step systematic design model with explicit dependency tracking and criterion-referenced assessment; and RPISD-Agent implements Rapid Prototyping ISD with K=3 refinement cycles prioritizing early prototype generation over comprehensive upfront analysis.
requirements: Agents require a base LLM (evaluated with Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-mini, Solar-Pro3) and tool definitions corresponding to their ISD theory's phases or steps
constraints: RPISD-Agent's approach is optimized for time-constrained scenarios where rapid delivery outweighs exhaustive planning; ADDIE-Agent's fine-grained decomposition incurs higher computational overhead
target_learners: Instructional designers and educational program developers across corporate, higher-education, and K-12 contexts
target_learning_goals: Automating the full instructional systems design lifecycle from needs analysis through evaluation
examples: React-ADDIE generates a thought, executes the phase tool, and observes the result at each ADDIE phase, encapsulating complete reasoning for an entire phase within a single LLM call

article_title: Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity
citation: Wong, S. S. H., & Qiu, S. X. (2026). Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10118-7
title: ISAR model: four types of AI effects on learning
description: The ISAR model proposed by Bauer et al. (2025) distinguishes four types of effects AI can exert on learning: inversion (AI leads to reduced cognitive processing and learning), substitution (AI provides instructional equivalence without changing cognitive processing), augmentation (AI enhances instruction with additional support without necessarily deepening processing), and redefinition (AI fosters deep constructive or interactive processes to enhance learning). The present study's findings align with the distinction between shallow appropriation (inversion-like) and deep collaborative engagement (redefinition-like) effects of AI.
requirements: Distinguishing between performance on assisted tasks and learning on subsequent unassisted tasks to classify AI effects
constraints: The model is cited from Bauer et al. (2025) as background; the present article tests its redefinition-type prediction only in creative problem-solving with university students
examples: The article frames free ChatGPT use that yields assisted-task gains but no unassisted gains as reliance rather than learning, and the guided approach as fostering deep constructive interaction

description: The review enumerates the ways virtual labs and computer simulation-based labs develop CT among biological science students: problem solving and hypothesis testing, application of theoretical knowledge, decision-making under constraints, development of inquiry-based skills via 'what if' features, enhanced observing and analyzing ability, feedback and reflection, collaboration and communication, integration of cross-disciplinary knowledge, and promoting creativity. article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: The isolated-interacting elements two-phase instructional approach
description: The thesis develops a two-phase instructional approach for complex material. In the first phase the material's element interactivity is artificially reduced by presenting information as isolated elements that can be processed serially rather than simultaneously in working memory; in the second phase all the information for understanding is presented. The control instruction presented all information for understanding in both phases. The approach aims to promote schema construction in order to foster understanding while avoiding early working-memory overload.
requirements: Complex material whose element interactivity can be analysed and artificially reduced in a first instructional phase
A second phase in which all the information required for understanding is presented
constraints: A possible consequence of artificially reducing element interactivity may be an initial decrease in a student's capacity for understanding, per the thesis's own hypothesis statement
target_learners: Novice students learning complex information (e.g. apprentices at the Email training centre and BHP Ltd.)
target_learning_goals: Understanding of complex, high element-interactivity content and schema construction
examples: Experiments 1 and 2 used isolated and interacting elements instructional materials; Experiments 3 and 4 used oven baking and oven electrical circuit materials; Experiment 5 used fault finding tests

article_title: Isolated and interrelated concepts
citation: Goldstone, R. L. (1996). Isolated and interrelated concepts. Memory & Cognition, 24 (5), 608-628. http://cognitrn.PSYCH-indiana.edu
title: Continuum of conceptual interrelatedness with converging manipulations and diagnostics
description: A framework placing concepts on a continuum from purely isolated (independent detectors or templates/prototypes) to purely interrelated (characterizations defined relative to competitor concepts). A concept "is interrelated with respect to another concept to the extent that its char­acterization is influenced by the other concept." The article operationalizes the continuum via three manipulations (instructions, category alternation frequency, labels) and two indicators (nondiagnostic-feature use; prototype vs. caricature categorization), using converging operations, and proposes a connectionist model in which interrelation depends on connection strength.
requirements: Converging operations: confidence in the construct increases only because manipulations and indicators provide mutually consistent results
constraints: The methods diagnose only interrelatedness arising from competition between mutually exclusive, simultaneously acquired artificial categories; semantic-association and theory-cohabitation interrelations were not evaluated
target_learners: adult laboratory learners of artificial categories
examples: Experiment 1 used imagery versus discriminating-feature instructions; Experiment 2 varied alternation frequency; Experiment 3 used symmetric versus negation labels; a connectionist simulation was presented to model intermediate degrees of interrelation

article_title: Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age
citation: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org
title: The isolation of knowledge as a critique of knowledge-based assessment
description: The report argues the construct of knowledge is a mismatch for the practical aims of assessment because of what the authors call the isolation of knowledge: "it is isolated from the bulk of social science research; as a description of a mental state, it is isolated from context; and perhaps worst of all, as an organization of information, it is isolated from the rest of the person." Most social sciences focus on choice rather than knowledge, so knowledge-based assessment cannot connect to social processes or to outcomes such as motivation and responses to feedback. The authors present this as a one-sided argument to dethrone knowledge as the central assessed outcome.
requirements: An alternative assessment frame must capture outcomes knowledge tests miss, such as motivations to learn, responses to feedback and change, and abilities to learn when no longer being told what to do
constraints: The authors acknowledge measuring what a student knows helps decide what to do next during instruction and remains essential for repetitive tasks such as licensing drivers
target_learners: Students in formal schooling assessed by current knowledge-based tests
target_learning_goals: Aligning assessment with preparation for life beyond specific trained tasks
examples: The report traces the history of assessment purposes from Binet's intelligence testing through behaviorist performance measures to cognitive knowledge assessment

title: iSTART-ME game-based intelligent tutoring system with four logged interaction categories
description: iSTART-ME (Interactive Strategy Training for Active Reading and Thinking - Motivationally Enhanced) is a game-based ITS that teaches self-explanation and comprehension strategies for complex science texts through introduction, demonstration, and extended practice modules. article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: The integrated Self-Regulated Learning (iSRL) model situating SRL in hierarchically nested ecological contexts with limited self-regulatory capacity
description: The iSRL model draws on social and clinical sciences to situate SRL within the broader life-context of the individual, applying "an ecological assets perspective" so that learning tasks are nested within courses, disciplines, schools, neighborhoods, and policies. It posits that self-regulatory capacity is a depleteable resource (ego depletion), so regulation of non-learning demands competes with SRL for limited resources. The model holds that "there are mutual and dynamic influences between one's ecological assets and one's ability to learn".
requirements: Researchers adopting the framework must account for unique and interactive influences of distal contextual factors on SRL in the immediate task
constraints: There is a scarcity of empirical work examining how individuals regulate learning while also accounting for additional cognitive processes unrelated to learning
target_learners: students across educational levels, including those facing unstable home environments
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting self-regulated learning within learners' broader life contexts
examples: The article illustrates depletion with a hungry child regulating hunger, addressed by school breakfast programs, and a student coping with an unstable home environment arriving at school with fewer resources to self-regulate learning

citation: Bauer, E., Greiff, S., Graesser, A. C., Scheiter, K., & Sailer, M. (2025). Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10020-8
title: ISAR model of four types of AI effects on learning: inversion, substitution, augmentation, and redefinition
description: The ISAR model classifies four types of AI effects on learning compared to non-AI conditions. It builds on the SAMR model and an ICAP-inspired SAMR model, retaining substitution, augmentation, and redefinition as mechanisms the authors say were 'empirically supported by a second-order meta-analysis on technology-enhanced learning', and adds inversion effects, 'referring to reduced cognitive learning when learners over-rely on AI'. The model is used to classify AI implementations and define research directions for AI-enhanced learning.
requirements: Requires explicit comparison conditions to assess when and where AI provides instructional benefits over non-AI-enhanced instruction
constraints: The article states the model's assumption is that the greater the instructional enhancement relative to a comparison condition, the greater the transformative potential, but implementations must avoid inversion effects
target_learning_goals: cognitive learning processes and outcomes, including knowledge and skills

title: ISEE Assessment human-flourishing framework built on Aristotle's eudaimonia
description: The ISEE Assessment's conceptual framework defines the purpose of education as human flourishing rather than economic growth, built on Aristotle's concept of "eudaimonia, loosely translated as 'flourishing.'" It defines flourishing, learning, evaluation and education through transdisciplinary review and consensual discussion, resting on the idea that education must ensure holistic development nurturing both human relationships and academic growth, aligned with Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It contrasts this with human capital theory, traditionally considered the primary educational goal for economic growth.
requirements: Working definitions of flourishing, learning, learner advancement and education established through transdisciplinary research review and consensual discussion among working groups
constraints: The paper states it does not encompass all recommendations from the original assessment, which are detailed in the report and policy briefs

target_learning_goals: holistic development for human flourishing and well-being
examples: The framework underpins the paper's three findings: the CASE approach, potentiality-based assessment, and the evolving role of technology

description: The editors define ISLG as a field of interest within AIEd characterized by four dimensions named for the abbreviation's letters: intelligent technologies, support offered, learning applications, and group characteristics. They argue the combination is broad rather than narrow: "While at first look, it may be seem that the scope of this field is extremely narrow, due to the constraints of combining these four dimensions, it is in fact the contrary." Each dimension is elaborated as an axis for characterizing any ISLG work.

description: The performance threshold is a global metacognitive support within iSTART's generative games. title: ISBAR framework for structured clinical handover
description: ISBAR (Introduction, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) is described as the most internationally recognized structured handover tool, whose five components guide nurses in transmitting and receiving cognition about a patient's current condition. The framework guides both the sender and receiver of handover to communicate systematically according to the patient's condition, helping to reduce the omission of critical information, eliminate irrelevant content and enhance continuity of care. In this study it served as the organizing structure for a simulation-based teaching intervention in obstetric nursing education.

examples: The intervention covered definitions, significance and clinical application of ISBAR in a 2-h didactic session with expert modelling

title: Incorporate structured, scenario-based ISBAR handover practice into specialist nursing curricula, particularly in high-risk areas
description: The article recommends that nursing educators incorporate ISBAR-structured simulation practice into specialist nursing curricula, particularly in high-risk areas such as obstetrics. It argues that the development of handover competence should not rely on incidental practice opportunities during clinical placements; instead, planned, progressive development should be undertaken before clinical placement through a four-stage design of didactic instruction, role-play, scenario simulation and OSCE. Learning in a low-risk professional environment helps students build a sense of achievement and internalize skills.
requirements: Planned, progressive development before clinical placement rather than reliance on incidental practice opportunities
constraints: The authors state that as this study employed a single-site, pre-experimental design, the four-stage sequence is offered as a potentially useful educational strategy rather than a validated model
target_learners: nursing students in specialist high-risk areas such as obstetrics
examples: The study implemented the four-phase design in an obstetric simulation and practicum course with 57 third-year nursing students

description: The article develops a blended MOOC implementation model using Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) with expert input from 15 participants. title: ISF-VSAQ: electronic immediate self-feedback very short answer question formative exam format
description: The ISF-VSAQ is an electronic formative exam item format developed at Phramongkutklao College of Medicine in which each item has "two sections with four parts", comprising a clinical vignette with response space and "expected answers with scores and self-scoring choices" on a 0.00–1.00 scale in 0.25 intervals, plus self-feedback on understanding (CU, PU, NU levels). title: I-ScaN: a longitudinal faculty POCUS training program with four elements
description: I-ScaN (Integrated Sonography Course at NYU) is a faculty development program for hospitalists consisting of "1.
